q1.question: How long does it take?
q1.answer: Typically 4-12 weeks depending on complexity. We provide clear timelines from the very start.

q2.question: Can I see the design before development?
q2.answer: Absolutely. We create full prototypes in Figma for your approval before development begins. You'll know exactly how your site will look.

q3.question: Can I update the content myself?
q3.answer: Yes, completely. We'll train you on the admin panel so you can easily update text, images, and content.

q4.question: What happens after the launch?
q4.answer: We offer maintenance and support plans. We’re always available for updates, optimizations, and troubleshooting.

q5.question: Is Google ranking (SEO) included?
q5.answer: We deliver your site with basic SEO implemented, optimized for speed and correct technical structure. For advanced SEO services to boost your traffic and ranking, we offer dedicated plans separately.

q6.question: What if I need specific functionalities?
q6.answer: We can design and integrate almost anything: payment gateways, booking systems, CRM integrations, automations, and more.

q7.question: How much does it cost to build a website in Lima, Peru?
q7.answer: At 3R Core, web design and development for US clients starts at $850 for landing pages and corporate sites up to 6 sections, including Figma design, responsive development, basic technical SEO, contact form and Google Analytics integration. Full corporate sites range from $1,200 to $2,500 and e-commerce from $2,000. In the first meeting we deliver an accurate quote based on your scope.

q8.question: How much does an online store (e-commerce) cost in Peru?
q8.answer: A professional online store with a catalog of up to 100 products, integrated payment gateway (Culqi, Niubiz, Izipay or Mercado Pago), inventory management and admin panel starts at $2,000 on Shopify or WooCommerce. SUNAT electronic invoicing, ERP integrations or multiple shipping methods raise the price according to complexity. Training is included so you can manage the store yourself.

q9.question: Which is better for my business: Shopify or WooCommerce?
q9.answer: Shopify works best if you want to launch fast, without worrying about hosting or technical maintenance, and you plan to sell between 50 and 5,000 products. WooCommerce (on WordPress) is better if you need maximum customization, full code control, specific ERP integrations or you already have content on WordPress. We work with both platforms: in the first meeting we recommend which one fits your Peruvian business model better.

q10.question: Does it include hosting, domain and SSL certificate?
q10.answer: The first year we include a .com or .pe domain, SSL certificate (Let's Encrypt or equivalent) and professional hosting at no additional cost as part of the package. From year 2 onwards hosting is billed separately ($8 to $35 per month depending on traffic and platform) or you can migrate it to your own provider with no penalty. Everything is registered under your name from day one.

q1.question: What does a digital marketing agency like 3R Core actually do?
q1.answer: We design websites, manage your social media, run Google Ads campaigns, position your brand on Google through SEO and develop your visual identity (branding). We work as your external marketing team: strategy + execution + monthly data-driven reports.

q2.question: Do you serve clients outside Lima or only in Peru?
q2.answer: We serve clients across Peru and the United States. We work remotely with video meetings and online reports. If your brand is outside Lima, no problem: 60% of our projects run 100% remotely.

q3.question: How much does it cost to hire a digital marketing agency in Lima?
q3.answer: It depends on the service and scope. As reference for US clients: our SEO plan starts at $500/month; Google Ads campaigns from $800/month + ad spend; social media management from $800/month; websites from $850. In our first meeting we deliver a tailored quote.

q4.question: How long does it take to see real results?
q4.answer: Google Ads and paid campaigns deliver results from month one. SEO and branding consolidate within 3 to 6 months. Social media management shows engagement impact from week 4. We give you clear KPIs from day one.

q5.question: Why choose 3R Core over another agency?
q5.answer: We are a 3-generation family agency (3R = the three Roque brothers) combining traditional experience with technology and digital-native vision. Every client works directly with a director, not a junior account. Transparent monthly reports and no forced long-term contracts.

q6.question: Do I need to have my brand ready or can you help me build it?
q6.answer: Both. If you already have branding, we respect it and build on top. If you start from scratch, our Branding team creates your logo, visual identity, brand book and every piece needed for your business to compete strongly online.

q7.question: How do I choose the best digital marketing agency in Lima?
q7.answer: Five filters that actually matter: 1) verifiable portfolio of projects similar to yours, 2) monthly reports with real metrics (not vanity metrics), 3) signed NDA and account ownership (your Google Ads, GA4 and social accounts stay yours), 4) a director joins the conversation, not just a junior account manager, and 5) real Google reviews and published case studies. At 3R Core we tick all 5.

q8.question: Should I hire an agency or several freelancers?
q8.answer: For small, very specific projects a freelancer can work. For a full strategy (brand + web + social + ads + SEO) an agency gives you coordination, a multidisciplinary team, continuity if someone leaves and a real process. Quick math: hiring 4 freelancers (designer, dev, community, ads specialist) usually costs the same or more than an agency, with zero coordination between them.

q9.question: How much should I invest monthly in digital marketing in Peru?
q9.answer: As a 2026 Lima reference: startups $750–1,400/month (covers social + basic ads), SMBs $1,500–3,600 (integrated strategy with social, ads, SEO and web improvements), mid-size companies $3,600–9,000 (full marketing with content production and CRO). What matters is not the budget itself but that ROI is positive by month 3.

q10.question: What happens to my Google Ads, Meta Ads and Analytics accounts if I leave the agency?
q10.answer: They are 100% yours, always. At 3R Core we create accounts under your name and we manage them with management permissions. If you decide to switch agencies or move in-house, you keep the entire history, creatives, saved audiences and full configuration. Zero locks.

q1.question: What is included in 3R Core's professional branding service?
q1.answer: Brand research, naming (if applicable), responsive logo design, corporate color palette, official typography, brand manual PDF, social media templates, corporate stationery (business cards, letterhead, envelopes), and brand applications on real mockups.

q2.question: How long does a complete branding project take?
q2.answer: We deliver a full branding project in 7 business days, with a clear milestone timeline: discovery, proposals, refinement and final delivery with all editable files. If the scope grows (corporate rebranding, extensive manuals, special applications) we agree on a longer timeline before kickoff.

q3.question: How much does designing my brand identity in Lima cost?
q3.answer: Branding projects at 3R Core start at $500 USD for US clients and scale according to corporate scope. We deliver a formal quote with detailed deliverables after an initial discovery session.

q4.question: If I only want a logo, can you do that?
q4.answer: Yes, we offer individual logo packages. However, we always recommend full branding: an isolated logo, without a visual system or manual, tends to lose strength and ends up being applied poorly across social media, web and ads.

q5.question: Will I receive the editable logo and brand manual files?
q5.answer: Yes, with no locks or restrictions. You receive vector files (.AI, .EPS, .SVG), .PDF for print, .PNG/.JPG for web, and the complete brand manual. The identity is 100% yours after delivery.

q6.question: Do you work with companies that already have a brand but want to redesign it?
q6.answer: Yes, we do rebranding and brand refresh. We audit the current identity, preserve valuable assets and modernize what no longer works. It's a more careful intervention because we must protect existing brand recognition.

q7.question: How do I choose a branding agency in Lima?
q7.answer: Always ask for 3 things before signing: 1) portfolio of projects in industries similar to yours, 2) written deliverables list (how many files, what formats, brand book length), and 3) timeline with clear milestones. A serious agency proposes a discovery session BEFORE quoting; a sloppy one throws a price without asking anything about your business.

q8.question: What's the difference between logo design, visual identity and branding?
q8.answer: Logo is just the icon/symbol. Visual identity is the full system (logo + colors + typography + iconography). Branding is the brand strategy (positioning, value proposition, tone of voice, architecture) plus that visual identity applied at every touchpoint. Asking for 'just a logo' is usually false economy: it ends up costing more when the entire visual system needs to be redone.

q9.question: What if I don't like any of the logo proposals?
q9.answer: We work with 2 included revision rounds: in the first we present 3 distinct concepts in black and white; we refine the chosen one in color and applications. If after the first round no concept convinces, we adjust the brief and iterate again at no additional cost. It's very rare: prior discovery gives us 80% of the work well-oriented.

q10.question: Does my brand need rebranding or just a refresh?
q10.answer: Refresh: if your logo looks dated but the brand is still recognized (modernize typography, simplify, adjust colors). Rebranding: if your value proposition changed, if the target audience is different, if you merged with another company, or if the brand has negative associations. We do a free initial audit and tell you which one applies.

intro.title: Why UGC beats polished production on cost per result
intro.p1: UGC is advertising shot to look like organic content: vertical, natural light, a real person talking to camera. It doesn't replace your brand film. It replaces the ad people scroll past.
intro.p2: The advantage is economic, not aesthetic. A traditional spot costs thousands and yields one asset. The same budget in UGC yields eight to twenty variations — and on platforms that optimize by creative, volume of variations is precisely what drives cost per result down.
intro.p3: We work with in-house creators in Lima, not a marketplace. That means we control the brief, the turnaround and the reshoot. If an angle underperforms, we shoot it again without renegotiating rates with a third party — and you get U.S.-agency output at nearshore cost.

q1.question: What exactly is UGC content?
q1.answer: It's paid advertising shot in the visual language of organic content: vertical format, natural light, a real person speaking to camera. It's produced specifically to run on Meta, TikTok and YouTube, and its advantage is that viewers consume it as a recommendation rather than an ad, which holds retention through the opening seconds where most ads lose the audience.

q2.question: How many videos do I need to start?
q2.answer: A first batch of six to ten assets is the practical minimum. Below that you have nothing to compare: if you test two videos and both underperform, you can't tell whether the format or the angle failed. With eight assets covering four distinct angles, the campaign tells you within two weeks which direction to push.

q3.question: Does UGC work for B2B or only consumer products?
q3.answer: Both, but the creator and the angle change. Consumer responds to demonstration and before/after. B2B responds to a usage testimonial, a specific operational problem explained plainly, and a comparison with the old way of doing things. What doesn't change is the principle: real face, direct tone, hook in the first seconds.

q4.question: Who owns the videos?
q4.answer: You do. The creator agreement assigns paid-media usage rights for the agreed term — typically twelve months, renewable — across the platforms we specify. We settle this in writing before filming, because putting real budget behind a video without documented rights is exactly the kind of exposure that surfaces once the campaign starts working.

q5.question: What's the turnaround on a batch?
q5.answer: Ten to fifteen business days from script approval to edited delivery. The slow part isn't filming, it's locking the angles. When the brief arrives with real customer objections already identified, delivery lands at the short end of that range.

q6.question: Can I run the same video on Meta and TikTok?
q6.answer: You can, but it underperforms. Each platform has its own grammar: TikTok rewards a spoken hook and fast cuts, Meta tolerates a slightly longer build and leans harder on captions. That's why we ship per-platform variations rather than one re-cropped master — force-cropping is the single most common way we've seen a good video underperform.

q7.question: How do I know if the UGC is working?
q7.answer: Three metrics, in this order: three-second retention tells you whether the hook works, click-through tells you whether the promise lands, and cost per acquisition tells you whether the angle sells. A video with strong retention and poor CPA isn't a bad video — it's a good hook on the wrong promise, and that gets fixed in the next script.

intro.p1: Most creator campaigns fail for the same reason: nobody defined what would be measured before spending. Reach gets paid for, posts go live, view counts get celebrated, and no one can say how many sales came in. That's not a campaign, it's an expense.
intro.p2: We invert the order. First we define the outcome — sales, sign-ups, qualified visits — then the attribution mechanism (tracked links, named discount codes, a dedicated landing page), and only then do we choose creators capable of producing it.
intro.p3: Selection runs on audience data, not the number on the profile. Where that audience lives, how old it is and how much real engagement it produces — because a 300,000-follower account whose audience sits outside your market sells you nothing.

q1.question: One large influencer or several smaller ones?
q1.answer: It depends on the objective. For launch awareness, a large account concentrates attention fast. For sales, several mid-tier creators usually perform better: proportional engagement is higher, rates are more negotiable, and splitting budget gives you several readings instead of one bet. When budget is limited, we almost always start with the second route.

q2.question: How do you verify an audience is real?
q2.answer: We cross several signals: engagement-to-follower ratio, how consistent that ratio is across posts, comment quality, declared audience location and historical growth pattern. Sharp step-shaped growth alongside generic comments is the classic purchased-audience signature, and it's enough to disqualify a profile no matter how impressive the reach looks.

q3.question: How is a sale attributed if the buyer doesn't purchase immediately?
q3.answer: Three complementary layers: a UTM-tagged link per creator, a named discount code, and a source question at checkout or on the form. None is perfect alone — people switch devices, watch a story and search the brand days later — but together they give attribution good enough to decide who to rebook.

q4.question: What does a creator campaign cost?
q4.answer: The range is wide because the variable is the deliverable, not the follower count. A mid-tier U.S. creator typically closes a story-plus-reel package between $300 and $2,500 depending on niche and exclusivity. What's worth budgeting isn't a single activation but a campaign across several creators and several posts, since an isolated mention rarely moves the needle.

q5.question: Can I use the creator's content in my ads?
q5.answer: Only if it's contracted. Paid-usage licensing is negotiated separately from the organic post and carries its own price, usually a percentage on top of the base rate for a defined term. We include it in the initial negotiation, because asking afterward — once the asset has proven it works — costs considerably more.

q6.question: What if the creator posts something off-brief?
q6.answer: The contract includes pre-publication review and a correction window. If the published asset misses the mandatory points, we request a correction or a repost; if that doesn't happen, payment is withheld as agreed. This clause rarely needs enforcing, but it's exactly what prevents disputes when something goes wrong.

q7.question: Does the partnership have to be disclosed?
q7.answer: Yes. In the United States, the FTC requires that material connections be disclosed clearly and conspicuously, and every platform provides a paid-partnership label for it. Beyond being mandatory, disclosure doesn't hurt performance: audiences already assume a commercial arrangement exists and respond well to it being stated.

q8.question: How long before results show?
q8.answer: Traffic peaks in the first 48 hours after each post, but the useful read comes at three to four weeks, once every creator has published and cost per result can be compared across them. Closing a campaign before that point usually means dropping creators who only needed a second post.

intro.p2: The common mistake is treating press like advertising. A journalist doesn't publish because your product is good — they publish because there's a story their audience cares about. Our job is to find that story inside your business and tell it in the form the outlet needs.

q1.question: What's the difference between PR and advertising?
q1.answer: In advertising you buy the space and control the message. In PR you earn the space and give up part of that control in exchange for credibility: the reader knows the outlet chose to publish it. That difference is exactly why an editorial mention carries more weight than an ad of the same size, and also why publication can never be guaranteed.

q2.question: Can you guarantee coverage in a specific outlet?
q2.answer: No, and be wary of anyone who does. What's guaranteed is the work: the media map, the angles, the materials, the outreach and the follow-up. The decision to publish belongs to the outlet. When someone guarantees a placement, what they're actually selling is paid space — a legitimate product, but a different one, with far less credibility value.

q3.question: What counts as news inside my company?
q3.answer: More than most people think, but almost never what the company wants to say. Launching a product isn't news. Proprietary data that reveals something about the market is. So is an industry figure nobody has published, a verifiable milestone, a contestable position, or a specific human story. Finding that inside the business is part of the work.

q4.question: Does PR help SEO?
q4.answer: Yes, two ways. First, links: a mention in an authoritative outlet is among the hardest links to earn and among the heaviest in weight. Second, brand: when people start searching your name after reading about you, Google reads those searches as a signal of a recognized entity, which benefits rankings across the whole domain.

q5.question: How long until results?
q5.answer: First coverage typically lands between weeks three and six, counting from when materials are ready. PR compounds: the second mention costs less effort than the first because the reporter already knows you, and from month three you start receiving inbound requests instead of only sending pitches.

q6.question: What happens during a reputation crisis?
q6.answer: The first rule is not improvising while it's hot. We establish verified facts, decide who speaks and through which channel, draft a position, and respond quickly but once — avoiding feeding the cycle. Most crises worsen not because of the original event but because of contradictory responses issued by several people in the first hours.

q7.question: Do you work with U.S. media?
q7.answer: Yes. Alongside Latin American press, we run coverage in U.S. and regional outlets, in English or Spanish depending on the target audience. For brands entering the U.S. market, English-language trade press usually opens more commercial doors than high-reach general press.

q8.question: How is a press campaign measured?
q8.answer: By mentions earned, outlet authority, links acquired, movement in branded search volume, and referral traffic. We report all five. Estimated reach, which many agencies present as the headline result, is the least reliable of the set and we don't use it as proof of success.
